newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries open higher before ECI, dollar cited.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries open higher before ECI, dollar cited.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries opened higher on Tuesday after a four-day losing streak, aided by dollar gains and awaiting the fourth-quarter Employment Cost Index (ECI) release.

"It's the dollar," said Raphael Marrone, money market economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. "Also, the market's sold off four days in a row in anticipation of a strong ECI number so some of that's been discounted -- and the market got a little short there, too."
But activity was light, Marrone said.
"There's not much going on; just thin trading," he said.
The Treasury market derived its strength from a dollar that opened near a 47-month high against the yen and a 31-month peak against the mark after breaking above 120 yen and 1.65 marks overnight.
Also, players said after its four-day selloff, the Treasury market had priced in a good part of any strong ECI reading.

Economists polled by Reuters estimated, on average, that the ECI, which gauges not only the cost of workers' wages, but also the cost of their benefits, rose 0.9 percent in the fourth quarter after a 0.6 percent rise in the third.
The ECI has drawn intense attention from the market ever since Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan referred to it in his July Humphrey-Hawkins testimony before Congress.

The ECI is a key inflation measure, according to economists, because labor accounts for two-thirds of the cost of producing goods. Rising labor costs must eventually find their way into the price of finished goods, they say, and therefore constitute inflationary pressure.
In early trade, the 6-1/2-percent 30-year benchmark Treasury bond was quoted up 7/32 at 94-21/32, its yield at 6.93 percent.

After a fourth-quarter of brisk economic activity, the inflation-wary bond market has become more intensely focused on the notion that inflation will accelerate and that the Federal Reserve will have to push interest rates higher to restrain the economy and forestall rising prices.
The Fed last changed monetary policy in January 1996, when it trimmed its target for the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to the current 5-1/4 percent.
But Raymond Worseck, chief economist at A.G. Edwards & Sons, said that one ECI reading is not enough to cause the Fed to hike official interest rates.

"Obviously, Greenspan watches everything, but I think the media sometimes gives the impression that if one number does one thing, he's going to throw out all the other pieces of data," said Worseck. "In the final analysis, he uses his judgment, which is what he should do."
But Josh Stiles, senior bond strategist at I.D.E.A., said the market's focus on the ECI was justified.

"Quite often, the market gets excessively hyped up before a number, but in my opinion, this really is an important number," he said. "It's a quarterly number and it's one that the Fed has emphasized as significant."
Traders said even after the market's four-day selling bout, the bond yield could climb still higher -- over seven percent -- if the ECI comes in at 1.0 percent or above.

Shortly before the ECI release, the two-year note was up 2/32 to 99-20/32, yielding 6.08 percent. The five-year note was up 4/32 to 99-10/32 to yield 6.41 percent. The 10-year was up 4/32 to 98-28/32, yielding 6.66 percent.
Three- and six-month bill rates were each down one basis point to 5.06 percent and 5.13 percent, respectively. Year bill rates were down two basis points to 5.31 percent.
